title: Mendel's laws and Punnett squares
blurb: Use the language of genetics, state Mendel's laws, and solve Punnett squares and probability questions for monohybrid, dihybrid and test crosses.
question: Two parents who do not have cystic fibrosis are both carriers of the recessive allele. Their first child has the disorder. What is the chance their next child will have it, and what is the chance that two children in a row would both have it?

teach.body: Gregor Mendel worked out the rules of heredity in the 1860s by crossing pea plants. Formal terms: a gene is a unit of heredity at a locus on a chromosome; an allele is one version of a gene (B or b); the genotype is the alleles present (BB, Bb, bb); the phenotype is the observable trait. Plain English: you carry two copies of each gene, one from each parent. Which copies you have is your genotype; what shows up is your phenotype.

Meaning
Example
rows: Two different alleles of one gene
Bb (a carrier if b causes disease)
Parents, offspring, F1 x F1 offspring

teach.body: 1. Law of segregation: each individual has two alleles per gene, and they separate during gamete formation (meiosis), so each gamete carries one allele. 2. Law of independent assortment: alleles of DIFFERENT genes sort into gametes independently of each other (true for genes on different chromosomes or far apart; linked genes break this rule). 3. Law of dominance: in a heterozygote, the dominant allele masks the recessive one.

children.label: Segregation
children.sub: 2 alleles of ONE gene split into gametes

teach.caption: Physical basis: homologs separate in anaphase I (segregation) and pairs line up independently in metaphase I (independent assortment). Dominance has no meiotic basis.

items: Write each parent's genotype (e.g. Aa x Aa).
Split each parent into its possible gametes (A or a) and place one parent across the top, the other down the side.
Fill each box with one allele from the top and one from the side.
Count the boxes: each of the 4 boxes is a 1/4 chance for EACH child.
Convert genotypes to phenotypes using the dominance rule.

teach.h: Aa x Aa: the monohybrid cross
teach.caption: Genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Phenotypes 3 dominant : 1 recessive (75% / 25%).

head: Cross
Genotypes
Phenotypes
teach.caption: Test cross: cross a dominant-looking individual with a homozygous recessive. Any recessive offspring prove the unknown parent is heterozygous.

teach.body: Ana and Luis Garcia are both carriers (Cc) of cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disorder. Cc x Cc gives 1 CC : 2 Cc : 1 cc, so each child has a 1/4 chance of cc. Their first child is affected, but each fertilization is independent: the next child's chance is still 1/4. The chance that two children in a row are both affected uses the product rule: 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16. The chance a child is a carrier (Cc) is 2/4 = 1/2.

teach.text: For Aa x Aa, 1:2:1 is the GENOTYPE ratio; the PHENOTYPE ratio is 3:1. A 3:1 ratio is a probability per child, not a promise that exactly 3 of 4 children will show the trait. Heterozygous means two different ALLELES of one gene, not two different genes. Segregation is about one gene's alleles; independent assortment is about different genes.

items: Genotype = alleles (BB, Bb, bb); phenotype = observable trait.
Segregation: one allele per gamete. Independent assortment: different genes sort separately. Dominance: dominant masks recessive.
Aa x Aa: 1:2:1 genotypes, 3:1 phenotypes. Test cross Aa x aa: 1:1. Dihybrid: 9:3:3:1.
Each child is an independent event; AND = multiply (product rule), OR = add (sum rule).
Probability of a heterozygous child from Aa x Aa = 1/2.

summary: You can now use gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, homozygous and heterozygous correctly, state Mendel's laws of segregation, independent assortment and dominance, and solve Punnett squares for monohybrid, test and dihybrid crosses. You can also apply the product rule and remember that every child is an independent event.

A.q: An individual has the genotype Bb for a single gene. Which term describes this genotype?
A.why: Bb has two different alleles of the same gene, so it is heterozygous.

whyNot.1: Homozygous dominant is BB: two identical dominant alleles.
whyNot.2: Homozygous recessive is bb: two identical recessive alleles.
whyNot.3: Hemizygous means having just one copy of a gene, as males do for X-linked genes.

A.q: Two pea plants heterozygous for height (Tt x Tt) are crossed. Tall (T) is dominant to short (t). Which phenotypic ratio is expected in the offspring?
A.why: Tt x Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; TT and Tt are both tall, so the phenotype ratio is 3 tall : 1 short.

whyNot.0: 1:2:1 is the GENOTYPE ratio, not the phenotype ratio.
whyNot.1: 1:1 is the result of a test cross (Tt x tt), not Tt x Tt.
whyNot.3: 2:1 miscounts the square: TT and both Tt boxes are tall, so 3 of 4 boxes are tall.

A.q: Which of Mendel's laws states that the two alleles for a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives one?
A.why: The law of segregation says the two alleles of a gene separate so each gamete carries only one.

whyNot.0: Independent assortment is about alleles of DIFFERENT genes sorting separately.
whyNot.1: The law of dominance says a dominant allele masks a recessive one in a heterozygote.
whyNot.2: Random fertilization adds variation but is not one of Mendel's laws.

B.q: A purple-flowered plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a white-flowered plant (pp). Half of the offspring have white flowers. What is the purple parent's genotype?
B.why: White (pp) offspring need a p from each parent, so the purple parent must carry p: it is Pp, and Pp x pp gives the 1:1 ratio seen.

whyNot.1: PP x pp would give all Pp offspring, all purple.
whyNot.2: A pp plant would have white flowers, not purple.
whyNot.3: The white offspring rule out PP, so the genotype can be determined: Pp.

B.q: Two parents are both Aa. What is the probability that their first two children are BOTH aa?
B.why: Each child has a 1/4 chance of aa. Independent events joined by AND are multiplied: 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16.

whyNot.0: 1/4 is the chance for ONE child; two children both aa requires multiplying.
whyNot.2: 1/8 would come from 1/4 x 1/2, but each child's chance of aa is 1/4.
whyNot.3: 3/16 (1/4 x 3/4) is the chance the first child is aa and the second is not.

B.q: In a cross of Aa x Aa, what is the probability that a child will be heterozygous?
B.why: Aa x Aa gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so 2 of 4 boxes (1/2) are heterozygous.

whyNot.0: 1/4 is the chance of AA or of aa, not Aa.
whyNot.1: 3/4 is the chance of the dominant PHENOTYPE (AA or Aa).
whyNot.3: 2/3 is the share of Aa among dominant-looking children only, not among all children.

C.q: Ana and Luis Garcia are both carriers (Cc) of cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disorder. Their first child has cystic fibrosis. What is the chance their next child will have it?
C.why: Each fertilization is independent, so every child of Cc x Cc has a 1/4 chance of being cc, whatever happened before.

whyNot.0: 1/2 is the chance of a carrier (Cc) child, not an affected one.
whyNot.1: 1/16 is the chance of two affected children in a row, asked before either is born.
whyNot.2: A 3:1 ratio is a probability for each child, not a quota that has been used up.

C.q: Two plants heterozygous for two genes on different chromosomes (AaBb x AaBb) are crossed. Both genes show complete dominance. What fraction of offspring show BOTH recessive traits?
C.why: The dihybrid ratio is 9:3:3:1; the 1 is aabb. Or multiply: 1/4 (aa) x 1/4 (bb) = 1/16.

whyNot.1: 3/16 is each of the two classes with one dominant and one recessive trait.
whyNot.3: 1/4 is the chance of ONE recessive trait (aa); both together is 1/4 x 1/4.

C.q: Which situation would NOT follow Mendel's law of independent assortment?
options: Two genes on two different chromosomes
Two genes close together on one chromosome
A heterozygote that shows the dominant trait
C.why: Genes close together on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, which violates independent assortment.

whyNot.0: Genes on different chromosomes are exactly the case where independent assortment holds.
whyNot.2: Homologs separating in anaphase I is the physical basis of the law of segregation, not an exception.
whyNot.3: A heterozygote showing the dominant trait follows the law of dominance.

reteach.title: Two decks of cards
reteach.question: Imagine each parent holds two cards for a trait and gives the child one card picked at random. How does that explain the 3:1 ratio?

blocks.body: Each parent holds two cards (alleles), say one A and one a. When making a gamete they hand over ONE card at random: that is segregation. The child ends up with one card from each parent. With two Aa parents, the four equally likely pairs are AA, Aa, aA and aa. Because A outranks a (dominance), three of those four pairs look dominant. Each new child is a fresh draw, so the odds reset every time.

blocks.text: A fresh draw every time: one affected child does not change the 1/4 odds for the next.

explain.body: Genotype is the pair of alleles (BB, Bb, bb). Phenotype is the trait you can observe (brown eyes). Different genotypes can share a phenotype: BB and Bb both look dominant. Environment, such as nutrition, can also affect phenotype.

explain.h: Two ways to describe a trait

test.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes genotype from phenotype?
options: Genotype is the trait; phenotype is the alleles
Genotype is dominant; phenotype is recessive
Genotype is the alleles; phenotype is the trait
Genotype is one allele; phenotype is two alleles
test.why: Genotype is the combination of alleles; phenotype is the observable trait those alleles produce.

whyNot.0: Reversed: alleles are the genotype, the trait is the phenotype.
whyNot.1: Dominant and recessive describe alleles, not the difference between genotype and phenotype.
whyNot.3: A genotype is a pair of alleles; a phenotype is the trait, not a number of alleles.

explain.body: Segregation: one gene's two alleles split into different gametes. Independent assortment: alleles of different genes sort separately (unless linked). Dominance: the dominant allele masks the recessive in a heterozygote.

test.q: Mendel's law of independent assortment states that:
options: The two alleles of one gene separate into different gametes
A dominant allele masks a recessive one in a heterozygote
Homologous chromosomes swap segments during prophase I
Alleles of different genes sort into gametes independently
test.why: Independent assortment: alleles of different genes are distributed to gametes independently of one another.

whyNot.0: That is the law of segregation, which concerns one gene.
whyNot.1: That is the law of dominance.
whyNot.2: That describes crossing over, which is not one of Mendel's laws.

explain.body: Put one parent's gametes across the top and the other's down the side; fill each box with one allele from each. Each box is a 1/4 chance. Convert genotypes to phenotypes with the dominance rule.

test.q: A homozygous dominant plant (AA) is crossed with a homozygous recessive plant (aa). Out of every 4 offspring, how many are expected to be heterozygous?
test.why: Every gamete from AA carries A and every gamete from aa carries a, so every offspring is Aa.

whyNot.1: 2 of 4 heterozygous comes from Aa x aa or AA x Aa, not AA x aa.
whyNot.2: 1 of 4 is the share of one homozygous class in Aa x Aa.
whyNot.3: 3 of 4 is the dominant phenotype share in Aa x Aa.

explain.body: A test cross mates a dominant-looking individual with a homozygous recessive. All dominant offspring suggests AA; any recessive offspring proves Aa. For probability, AND means multiply, OR means add, and each child is independent.

test.q: What is the main purpose of a test cross?
options: To cross two heterozygotes to get a 3:1 ratio
To tell if a dominant-looking parent is AA or Aa
To tell if a recessive-looking parent is aa or Aa
To make an F1 generation that is all heterozygous
test.why: Crossing the unknown with a homozygous recessive reveals whether it carries a hidden recessive allele.

whyNot.0: A test cross uses a homozygous recessive partner, not two heterozygotes.
whyNot.2: A recessive phenotype can only be aa, so its genotype is already known.
whyNot.3: Crossing AA with aa to get an all-Aa F1 is a parental (P) cross; a test cross is used to reveal an unknown genotype.
